newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nail bomb attack on Nigerian military wounds eight.
newsitem.headline: Nail bomb attack on Nigerian military wounds eight.

text.p: A bomb packed with nails blasted a military bus in a Lagos street on Wednesday, wounding eight people, five of them Nigerian soldiers, the state police chief said.
It is the fourth attack since December on the military which has ruled politically-volatile Nigeria for 26 out of 36 years of independence from Britain.
"The blast went off when the military bus was passing," police commissioner Abubakar Tsav told Reuters. "Five of the people injured are military, including a female soldier."
"Bomb disposal experts have recovered the device in todays explosion and it is similar to the ones used in previous attacks," Tsav said.
Similar blasts that have rocked Nigerias biggest city have been blamed by the police on the umbrella opposiion group, the National Democratic Coalition (NADECO) and its foreign based affiliates.

According to security agencies 22 people are in detention in connection with the blasts including Frederick Fasehun a former presidential aspirant and chairman of the Campaign for Democracy pressure group.
His associates deny he is involved.

Similarly the family of former finance minister Olu Falae, who also sought to contest the presidency and who is a top member of NADECO, say he has been detained since December over the bombings but deny he is involved.
Opposition activists have urged the government to look elsewhere including among dismissed or retired members of the armed forces for the culprits.
Tsav said among those injured was a motorcyclist who was riding by at the time.
He said: "The device recovered was fortified with four-inch nails, apparently to cause maximum damage but fortunately no one was killed. Only one person has serious injuries."
A bomb blasted an army bus in Lagos in January killing three soldiers and wounding dozens of others.
In December, two bombs exploded within days targeting the military administrator of Lagos state, Colonel Muhammed Marwa, a close aide of military ruler General Sani Abacha.
Nigeria has been in crisis since a previous military ruler in 1993 annulled elections that would have restored democracy.

Abacha, who seized power in the aftermath of the annulment promises to hand over to a democratically-elected president next year and on Monday a 10-day registration of voters for elections starting from March commenced nationwide.

The opposition, however, dismiss the transition to democracy as a ruse to perpetuate Abachas rule and point to a recent interview in which he did not exclude himself out from contesting next years presidential election.
They also point to the continued detention of opposition figures such Moshood Abiola, the wealthy businessman presumed to have won the annulled 1993 presidential poll.

Nigeria is treated as a pariah over its human rights record and the 1995 hanging on murder charges of nine minority rights activists from the Ogoni tribe including writer Ken Saro-Wiwa. The executions prompted the Commonwealth to suspend Nigeria.
